newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers parade in show of force.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers parade in show of force.

text.p: Farmers drove 2,000 tractors onto Greece's main north-south highway on Thursday in show of force after Prime Minister Costas Simitis refused to meet them to discuss their demands.
The farmers took their tractors through cotton fields and across rivers to emerge on the national highway in the Almiros region south of the central town of Larissa, the headquarters of their revolt.
It was yet another humilation for 5,000 police, many in riot gear, who had strict orders from Simitis to prevent the farmers and their tractors from taking over the roads.
The tractor onvoy, stretching many kilometres, rattled along the highway as police watched from a distance, unable to react.
"This will show Mr Simitis that we mean business," said Nikos Harmouzis, a cotton grower in the convoy.
"We know that we will meet riot units further down but we don't want to clash with police. We'll decide later whether we will stay on the road all night."
Simitis earlier rejected a farmers' request to meet their representatives, saying no meeting was possible with the roads under siege.
The government, which has faced almost continuous strikes and protests against its strict ecomomic policies since coming to power in September, said it would not accept an ultimatum.
"All forms of mobilisation and threats to close off the roads must clearly stop for such a meeting to be possible," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters.

The farmers have played a hide-and-seek game with police for three days, driving their tractors off the roads and across farmland or under bridges whenever riot squads and police helicopters confronted them.
They blocked minor roads to try to show that police could not stop them from repeating a crippling road blockade that virtually cut Greece in two in December.
Simitis successfully waited out that 25-day blockade, saying the country could not afford to satisfy their demands, which include cheaper fuel, lower taxes and more subsidies.
The farmer are among a long list of groups protesting or striking against a 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, and strict incomes and tax policies.
Teachers are on strike for a third week while labour confederations have staged repeated walkouts. Protest rallies snarl up traffic in Athens almost every day.
Simitis has icely turned down all labour demands, saying that to give in would jeopardise Greece's efforts to catch up economically with its European Union partners.
